summary.text: For \(n>122\), positivity of the count yields a twin-prime pair lying strictly between the consecutive squares, so its smaller member is a prime in the desired interval. The remaining cases \(1\le n\le122\) are settled by an explicit finite list of prime witnesses, one for each interval.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S_n=\left\{p\in\mathbb N:
 n^2+1\le p\le (n+1)^2-3,\quad p\text{ is prime},\quad p+2\text{ is prime}
\right\}.
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is defined by
\[
a(n)=|S_n|.
\]
For the values of \(n\) relevant below, \((n+1)^2\ge 3\), and the upper-bound condition can be read in the usual integer sense. Namely,
\[
p\le (n+1)^2-3
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
p+2<(n+1)^2.
\]
The lower bound similarly gives \(n^2<p\). Hence an element of \(S_n\) is the first member of a twin-prime pair lying entirely strictly between the two consecutive squares. In particular, the first member alone is a prime strictly between those squares.

Assume the hypothesis
\[
\forall n>122,
\qquad a(n)>0.
\tag{1}
\]
We prove that for every positive integer \(n\), there is a prime strictly between \(n^2\) and \((n+1)^2\).

We first record the finite part of the argument. For every \(n\) with \(1\le n\le122\), the following table gives a prime \(q_n\) satisfying
\[
n^2<q_n<(n+1)^2.
\tag{2}
\]

\[
\begin{array}{c|r@{\qquad}c|r@{\qquad}c|r@{\qquad}c|r}

\]

Here is how the finite assertions represented by the table are established. In each row one directly squares \(n\) and \(n+1\) and checks the two strict inequalities in (2). Each listed number is prime by trial division: for a listed integer \(q\), divide by every prime \(r\le\sqrt q\); none has remainder zero. This is a complete primality test. Indeed, if \(q\) were composite, write \(q=uv\) with \(1<u\le v\). Then \(u^2\le uv=q\), so \(u\le\sqrt q\), and some prime divisor of \(u\) would be a prime divisor of \(q\) no larger than \(\sqrt q\), contrary to the divisions. Thus the table proves (2) for all 122 values and supplies the required finite Legendre check.

Now fix an arbitrary positive integer \(n\). There are two cases.

First suppose \(n\le122\). The entry \(q_n\) in the table is prime and satisfies
\[
n^2<q_n<(n+1)^2,
\]
so it is the desired prime.

It remains to consider \(n>122\). By (1), \(a(n)>0\). Since \(a(n)\) is the cardinality of the finite set \(S_n\), a positive cardinality means that \(S_n\) is nonempty. Choose \(p\in S_n\). Unpacking membership in \(S_n\), we have
\[
p\text{ prime},\qquad p+2\text{ prime},
\tag{3}
\]
and
\[
n^2+1\le p\le (n+1)^2-3.
\tag{4}
\]
The first inequality in (4) implies \(n^2<p\). For the upper inequality, set \(M=(n+1)^2\). Since \(n>122\), certainly \(M\ge3\), so there is no truncation issue in \(M-3\). From \(p\le M-3\) we obtain
\[
p+3\le M,
\]
and therefore \(p<M=(n+1)^2\). Consequently
\[
n^2<p<(n+1)^2.
\]
Together with the primality of \(p\) from (3), this gives the required prime. (The primality of \(p+2\), while responsible for the fact that the counted object is a twin-prime pair, is more than is needed for Legendre’s conclusion.)

Every positive integer \(n\) is either at most \(122\) or greater than \(122\), and the two cases above cover both possibilities. Hence, under the assumption that \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>122\), for every positive integer \(n\) there exists a prime \(p\) with
\[
n^2<p<(n+1)^2.
\]
This is Legendre’s conjecture.
